title: Central Idea and Evidence
bigQuestion: How do you find what a piece of nonfiction is really saying, and how do you know whether to trust it?

story.title: One Block Apart, Two Different Fires
story.kicker: On the night of October 8, 1871, Chicago began to burn. Two neighbors watched the same flames and wrote two very different accounts.
paragraphs: The Great Chicago Fire started on the evening of Sunday, October 8, 1871, in a barn on DeKoven Street on the city's near southwest side. The summer had been dry, the wind was strong, and most of the city was built of wood. By the time rain finally put the fire out on October 10, about three hundred people were dead, roughly a hundred thousand had lost their homes, and more than three square miles of the city were ash. The old stone Water Tower on Michigan Avenue still stands today, one of the few buildings that survived.

Now picture two neighbors who lived a block apart that night. Their letters are imagined for this chapter, but people like them were real. The first neighbor, a tailor, writes to his brother: "The wind carried burning boards over our heads like leaves. I put my wife and the children in a cart and pushed them north for two hours. Behind us the sky was orange. I did not look back until we reached the river."

The second neighbor, a schoolteacher, writes in her diary: "The fire bells rang for an hour before anyone in our building moved. The firemen were exhausted from a large blaze the night before. If the city had kept more engines on the west side, the fire would have been stopped at the river. This was not bad luck. This was bad planning."

Read the two accounts again. The tailor tells you what he saw and felt. His central idea is something like: the fire was terrifying and we barely escaped. The teacher tells you what she thinks caused the disaster. Her central idea is: the city could have stopped this fire. Same night, same block, two central ideas.

Both accounts are useful. Neither is the whole story. A good reader of nonfiction does what a detective does: finds the main point of each account, checks which details support it, notices the writer's tone and purpose, and then compares the accounts to get closer to what really happened. That is the work of this chapter.
story.think: Which neighbor's account would you trust more if you wanted to know what the fire felt like? Which one if you wanted to know what caused it to spread? Why?

lessons.title: Topic Is Not the Same as Idea
lessons.mainIdea: A topic is what a text is about; the central idea is what the text says about that topic, and it is always a full sentence.
reading: Ask a student what an article is about and you may hear one word: "Sharks." That word is the *topic*. But a text is never just about sharks. It says something about sharks. "Most shark species are harmless to people" is a sentence. That sentence is the *central idea*: the main point the writer wants you to take away. A topic is a word or phrase. A central idea is a whole sentence with a claim in it.

Here is a short paragraph written for this lesson. "Chicago's Water Tower looks like a small castle, but it was built in 1869 to hold a tall standpipe that evened out the pressure of water pumped from Lake Michigan. When the Great Fire burned the neighborhood around it in 1871, its limestone walls did not burn. Today it stands on Michigan Avenue as a reminder of the city that rebuilt itself." The topic is the Water Tower. The central idea is bigger: a plain working building became a symbol of Chicago's survival.

To find the central idea, ask two questions. First: what is this mostly about? That gives you the topic. Second: what does the writer most want me to understand about it? Answer in a full sentence, and you have the central idea. Longer texts can have more than one central idea, one per section, and one bigger idea that ties them together.

Watch out for a common mistake. A single interesting detail is not the central idea. "The Water Tower was built in 1869" is true and specific, but the paragraph is not mostly about that date. The central idea has to cover most of the details in the text, not just one of them.

words.d: what a text is about, said in a word or short phrase
the main point a nonfiction text makes about its topic, stated as a full sentence
a specific fact, example or description that supports a central idea

look.title: Three Sentences, One Central Idea
look.text: A paragraph says: Monarch butterflies fly up to 3,000 miles from Canada to Mexico each fall. No single butterfly makes the whole round trip; it takes several generations. Scientists still do not fully understand how the young butterflies find a place they have never seen.
look.prompt: What is the topic? Now write the central idea as one full sentence that covers all three details.

check.q: Which of these is a central idea, not just a topic?
choices: The Water Tower became a symbol of a city that rebuilt itself
check.why: A central idea is a full sentence that says something about the topic. The other choices are only topics or details.

check.q: Why is "The Water Tower was built in 1869" not the central idea of the model paragraph?
choices: It is one detail, and the central idea has to cover most of the details
It has a number in it
check.why: One detail, even a true one, is not the main point. The central idea covers most of what the text says.

check.q: What is the second question you ask to find a central idea?
choices: What does the writer most want me to understand about the topic?
check.why: The first question finds the topic. The second finds what the writer says about that topic, which is the central idea.

lessons.title: How Details Build an Idea
lessons.mainIdea: Writers develop a central idea with details such as facts, examples, numbers and quotations, and each detail should push the idea forward.
reading: A central idea with no details is just a claim floating in the air. "Lake Michigan is dangerous for swimmers." Says who? Now add details. "Rip currents form along Chicago's beaches when waves pile water against the shore. In some summers, more people drown in Lake Michigan than in any other Great Lake. Lifeguards fly red flags on days when the current is strong." Now the idea has legs to stand on.

Nonfiction writers use a small set of detail types again and again. Facts: things that can be checked. Numbers and statistics: counts and measurements. Examples: one specific case that shows the idea. Quotations: the words of a person who knows. Descriptions: what something looks or sounds like. When you read, label the details. It helps you see how the writer is building.

Good writers do not pile up details at random. Each one *develops* the idea, meaning it adds a new piece. In the lake paragraph, the first detail explains how the danger happens, the second shows how serious it is, and the third shows what people do about it. Take one detail away and the idea gets weaker. That is the test of a detail that belongs.

Try this when you read a paragraph: draw a line, put the central idea at the top, and hang each detail under it. If a detail does not hang from the idea, either the writer wandered or you have the wrong central idea. Both are worth noticing.

words.d: to build an idea up by adding details that make it fuller and clearer
a number that comes from counting or measuring something
the exact words someone said or wrote, set inside quotation marks

look.title: Details in a Model Paragraph
look.cite: A seven-sentence paragraph on rip currents, written and counted for this lesson
look.prompt: This writer used mostly facts and numbers. What kind of central idea might need more quotations or examples instead?

check.q: What does a detail do for a central idea?
choices: It supports and builds the idea
It makes the text longer for no reason
check.why: Details develop the central idea by giving it facts, examples and other support.

check.q: Which of these is a statistic?
choices: The lake was gray and cold
Rip currents form when waves push water against the shore
check.why: A statistic is a number from counting or measuring. Twelve people is a count.

check.q: You find a detail that does not connect to the central idea you wrote down. What might that mean?
choices: You may have the wrong central idea, or the writer wandered
The text has no central idea
You should skip the rest of the text
check.why: Every detail should hang from the central idea. A loose detail is a sign to check your idea or the writer's focus.

lessons.title: The Objective Summary
lessons.mainIdea: An objective summary restates a text's central idea and key details in your own words, without adding your opinion.
reading: Your friend missed the article and asks what it said. You could read it aloud, but that would take ten minutes. Instead you say: "It's about rip currents in Lake Michigan. They form when waves push water against the beach, they cause more drownings than people expect, and lifeguards use flags to warn swimmers." That is a *summary*: the central idea plus the key details, shorter, in your own words.

Now notice what you did not say. You did not say "and I think swimming there is stupid." That is your opinion, and it does not belong in an *objective* summary. Objective means you keep yourself out of it. You report what the writer said, not what you think about it. A test: if the writer read your summary, they should nod and say "yes, that is what I wrote."

Here is a way to build one. Start with the central idea in one sentence. Add the two or three details that matter most, in the order the writer used. Leave out small examples, jokes and repeated points. Use your own words, except for a key term you cannot replace. Keep it to about a quarter of the original length, or less.

A summary is not a list of everything, and it is not a review. "This article was boring" is a review. "The article explains how rip currents form and how to stay safe" is a summary. Learning the difference will help you in every class where a teacher says "tell me what you read."

words.d: a short restatement of a text's central idea and most important details
based on the facts of the text, with no personal opinion added

look.title: Which One Is Objective?
look.text: Two students summarize the same article about the Chicago Water Tower. Ana: "The article says the Water Tower was built in 1869 to hold a standpipe, survived the 1871 fire, and became a symbol of the city." Deshawn: "The article says the Water Tower is the coolest building in Chicago and everyone should visit it."
look.prompt: Which summary is objective? What did the other student add that the writer probably never said?

check.q: Which sentence belongs in an objective summary?
choices: I think the writer is wrong about the lake
This was the best article I read all year
Rip currents form when waves push water against the shore
Everyone should be scared of the lake
check.why: An objective summary restates what the text says. The other choices are opinions or reviews.

check.q: About how long should a summary be compared with the original?
check.why: A summary is much shorter than the text, usually a quarter of the length or less.

check.q: Why should you use your own words in a summary?
choices: Because the writer's words are always wrong
Because copying sentences shows you did not understand the idea
Because your teacher cannot read the original
check.why: Restating in your own words proves you understood the idea, not just copied it.

lessons.title: Four Ways to Organize
lessons.mainIdea: Nonfiction writers organize text in patterns such as time order, cause and effect, compare and contrast, and problem and solution, and signal words reveal the pattern.
reading: Read this: "First the barn caught fire. Then the wind carried sparks to the next block. By midnight the fire had jumped the river." The writer is telling events in the order they happened. That pattern is *chronological* order, or time order. Signal words like first, then, next, by midnight and finally give it away.

Now read this: "Because the summer had been dry and the buildings were wood, the fire spread fast. As a result, the fire department could not keep up." This is *cause and effect*: one thing makes another thing happen. Signal words: because, so, as a result, therefore, led to. A writer uses this pattern to explain why something happened.

Two more patterns are common. *Compare and contrast* shows how two things are alike and different: "Both letters describe the fire, but the tailor focuses on fear while the teacher focuses on blame." Signal words: both, similarly, however, on the other hand, unlike. *Problem and solution* names a difficulty and then how it was fixed: "After the fire, Chicago faced a housing crisis. The city answered with new building codes and brick construction." Signal words: problem, solution, answer, solved.

Most long texts mix patterns. An article might tell a story in time order, pause to explain a cause, then compare two responses. Your job is to notice the pattern in each part. Once you see the shape, the details fall into place and the text is much easier to remember.

words.d: arranged in the order that events happened in time
a pattern that shows how one thing makes another thing happen
a pattern that shows how two things are alike and different
a word or phrase, such as because or however, that shows how ideas connect

look.title: Name the Pattern
look.text: Paragraph A: Unlike the North Side, which was rebuilt in brick within a few years, parts of the West Side kept wooden houses for decades. Paragraph B: The city lacked clean water after the fire, so engineers built a new pumping station beside the Water Tower.
look.prompt: Which pattern does each paragraph use? Which signal words told you?

check.q: Which words signal cause and effect?
check.why: Because, as a result and therefore show that one thing made another happen.

check.q: "The tailor focused on fear while the teacher focused on blame." What pattern is this?
check.why: The sentence shows how two accounts differ. That is compare and contrast.

check.q: Why do writers use chronological order?
choices: To show how two things are alike
To offer a fix for a difficulty
To tell events in the order they happened
check.why: Chronological order follows time. It is the pattern for telling what happened step by step.

lessons.title: Why This Order?
lessons.mainIdea: Analyzing structure means asking why a writer put a paragraph or section where it is, and what the text would lose if it moved.
reading: Knowing the pattern is step one. Step two is asking why. A writer chooses where every paragraph goes. An article about the fire could start with the death toll, or with a single family in a cart, or with the dry summer that set the stage. Each choice does a different job. Starting with the family pulls you in. Starting with the death toll shocks you. Starting with the weather prepares you to understand the cause.

Here is a model text written for this lesson. Its first paragraph describes a girl on a Chicago beach watching a red flag go up. Its second paragraph explains what a rip current is. Its third gives a drowning statistic. Its fourth tells swimmers what to do. Ask: why put the girl first? Because a reader cares about a person before a fact. Why put the statistic third and not first? Because after you understand the current, the number means more.

Now try moving a piece. Put the statistic first. The article becomes colder and more alarming. Put the advice first. Now the reader gets instructions before knowing why they matter. Neither is wrong, but each changes the reading. Noticing this is what teachers mean by *analyzing structure*: seeing that the order is a choice and explaining what the choice does.

When you write about structure, use sentences like these. "The writer opens with a story to make the reader care." "The writer saves the statistic until after the explanation so the number has meaning." "The final section gives advice, which turns fear into action." Every sentence names a part, its place, and its effect.

words.d: the way a text's parts are arranged and how they fit together
to break something into its parts and explain how the parts work

look.title: Move the Paragraph
look.text: An article about school lunches has four paragraphs: 1. A student describes a soggy tray. 2. The cost of a lunch and what the district gets from the state. 3. A comparison with a district that cooks fresh food. 4. Three changes the school board could vote on.
look.prompt: What would change for the reader if paragraph 4 came first? Why do you think the writer put the soggy tray first?

check.q: What does it mean to analyze a text's structure?
choices: To explain why the parts are arranged as they are and what that does
To rewrite the text in your own words
check.why: Analyzing structure means seeing the order as a choice and explaining its effect on the reader.

check.q: In the model text, why does the writer put the girl on the beach first?
choices: Because the writer forgot the statistic
Because a reader cares about a person before a fact
Because it is the shortest paragraph
check.why: Opening with a person draws the reader in. The facts come after the reader cares.

check.q: If the drowning statistic moved to the first paragraph, what would probably happen?
choices: The number would mean less to the reader
The article would be more alarming from the start
check.why: Starting with a shocking number changes the mood. The reading gets colder and more alarming right away.

lessons.title: Word Choice and Tone
lessons.mainIdea: Tone is the writer's attitude toward the subject, and you hear it in the exact words the writer chose.
reading: Read two sentences about the same event. "The fire department responded to the blaze." "The fire department crawled toward the blaze." Both say the firefighters went. But crawled tells you the writer thinks they were slow, maybe even blames them. Responded is neutral. One word changes the whole feeling. That feeling, the writer's attitude toward the subject, is the *tone*.

Tone shows up in nouns and verbs, not just adjectives. "The crowd gathered" is calm. "The mob swarmed" is frightened or scornful. "The mayor stated" is neutral. "The mayor insisted" hints that someone doubted him. "The mayor whined" is openly mocking. When you notice a word that could have been plainer, ask what the writer gained by choosing it.

Words also carry *connotation*, the feeling attached to a word beyond its plain meaning. Thrifty and cheap both mean careful with money, but thrifty sounds like praise and cheap sounds like an insult. Nonfiction writers who want to seem fair choose words with little connotation. Writers who want to persuade often reach for words with a lot of it. You can tell one from the other by listening.

Some tone words to keep handy: neutral, formal, serious, urgent, admiring, critical, sarcastic, playful, angry, hopeful. When a teacher asks about tone, pick one of these, then point to the two or three words in the text that create it. Tone is never a guess; it is evidence.

words.d: the writer's attitude toward the subject, shown through word choice
the feeling or idea a word carries beyond its plain dictionary meaning
showing no strong feeling for or against something

look.title: Two Accounts of One Storm
look.text: Version A: The storm passed through the county on Tuesday, taking down about forty trees and leaving some homes without power until morning. Version B: The storm tore through the county on Tuesday, ripping down forty trees and plunging helpless families into darkness for the whole night.
look.cite: Two versions of one report, written for this lesson
look.prompt: List the words that differ between A and B. What tone does each version have, and which would you trust more for the facts?

check.q: What is tone in nonfiction?
choices: The writer's attitude toward the subject
The date the text was written
check.why: Tone is the writer's attitude, and readers hear it in word choice.

check.q: "The mayor whined about the budget." What does the verb whined tell you?
choices: The writer is neutral about the mayor
The writer is mocking the mayor
The writer is quoting the mayor
check.why: Whined has a scornful connotation. It shows the writer looks down on the mayor's complaint.

check.q: A writer who wants to seem fair and factual will usually choose words that are
check.why: Neutral words let the facts speak. Loaded words show the writer is pushing a feeling.

lessons.title: Two Authors, One Topic
lessons.mainIdea: When two authors write about the same topic, compare what each includes, leaves out, and emphasizes, and you will understand the topic better than either author alone.
reading: Go back to the two neighbors. The tailor and the teacher stood a block apart and watched the same fire. One wrote about the terror of escape. The other wrote about the city's failures. Neither lied. Each chose what to include, what to leave out, and what to *emphasize*, meaning what to give the most space and the strongest words. Reading both gives you more than reading either one.

To compare two authors, make three columns. Column one: what does each author include that the other does not? The tailor mentions the cart and the children; the teacher mentions the fire bells and the tired firemen. Column two: what does each emphasize? The tailor emphasizes feelings; the teacher emphasizes causes. Column three: where do they agree? Both say the wind was fierce and the fire moved fast. Agreement between two separate witnesses is strong evidence.

Then ask why the accounts differ. Purpose matters: the tailor is writing to reassure a brother; the teacher is writing to work out her own anger. Position matters: someone fleeing sees different things than someone who stayed. Knowledge matters: the teacher may have read the newspaper and the tailor may not have. None of these make an author wrong, but they explain the shape of what each wrote.

In writing, a comparison sounds like this: "Both accounts describe a fast-moving fire, but the tailor's letter focuses on his family's escape while the teacher's diary blames the city's lack of preparation. Because the teacher had time to reflect, her account offers a cause; because the tailor was fleeing, his offers a scene." Name both, show the difference, explain the reason.

words.d: to give something extra attention or importance
a description of an event by someone who saw it or studied it
the position and experience from which a person sees something

look.title: Two Reports on One Game
look.text: Report A, from a home-team writer: "The Wolves fought hard but fell 3 to 2 after a questionable call in the final minute." Report B, from a visiting-team writer: "The Hawks earned a 3 to 2 win with a late goal that the Wolves' coach argued about for ten minutes."
look.prompt: What do both reports agree on? What does each one emphasize, and why might that be?

check.q: When two honest witnesses agree on a detail, that detail is
check.why: Two separate people reporting the same thing makes it more likely to be true.

check.q: What does it mean to emphasize something in a text?
choices: To put it in quotation marks
To give it extra attention and importance
check.why: Emphasizing means giving something more space or stronger words so the reader notices it.

check.q: Why did the teacher's account offer a cause while the tailor's offered a scene?
choices: The teacher had time to reflect and the tailor was fleeing
The tailor did not know how to write
The teacher was not really there
check.why: Position and purpose shape what a writer includes. Someone reflecting later can think about causes; someone escaping records what they saw.

lessons.title: Letters, Speeches and Diaries
lessons.mainIdea: A primary source is a text made by someone who was there, and it is powerful evidence as long as you remember who wrote it, for whom, and why.
reading: A history textbook about the Civil War was written a hundred and fifty years after it. A soldier's letter home was written the night after a battle. The letter is a *primary source*: a text created by someone who was there at the time. The textbook is a *secondary source*: a text that explains or interprets primary sources. Both are useful, but they are different kinds of evidence.

Primary sources come in many forms. Letters, diaries, speeches, photographs, newspaper reports from the day, laws, maps, and interviews with people who lived through an event. Each one was made for a reason. A letter was written to one person, so it may be honest but also private and one-sided. A speech was written for a crowd, so it is shaped to move that crowd. A diary was written for the writer alone, so it may say what no one else heard.

Read a primary source with three questions. Who made this? What did they want? Who was supposed to read or hear it? Abraham Lincoln's Gettysburg Address, given in November 1863, was a speech at the dedication of a cemetery for soldiers killed months earlier. Knowing that tells you why it is short, serious and full of words like dedicate, consecrate and devotion. The occasion shaped the words.

A primary source is not automatically true. A person who was there may have seen only a corner of the event, may have wanted to look good, or may simply have misremembered. Use the same skills you use on any text: find the central idea, check the details, notice the tone, and compare it with another account.

words.d: a text or object made by someone who was there when an event happened
a text that explains or interprets events using primary sources
the event or situation that a speech or piece of writing was made for

look.title: The First Sentence of a Famous Speech
look.text: Four score and seven years ago our fathers brought forth on this continent, a new nation, conceived in Liberty, and dedicated to the proposition that all men are created equal.
look.prompt: A score is twenty years. What year is Lincoln pointing back to, and why would he begin a cemetery speech in 1863 by counting back to that year?

check.q: Which of these is a primary source about the Chicago Fire?
choices: A website built in 2020 that explains the fire
A diary written by a Chicagoan in October 1871
check.why: A diary written at the time by someone who was there is a primary source. The others interpret events later.

check.q: Why might a speech and a diary about the same event sound different?
choices: Because speeches are never about real events
Because a speech is shaped for a crowd and a diary is written for the writer alone
check.why: Audience shapes the writing. A speech aims to move listeners; a diary can say private thoughts.

check.q: A primary source should be read
choices: as always true, because the writer was there
with the same care as any text, checking who wrote it and why
check.why: Being there does not make a writer correct or complete. Check the source like any other text.

lessons.title: Graphs and Pictures With the Words
lessons.mainIdea: Graphs, maps and photos carry information the words do not, and reading them well means checking labels, scale and what was left out.
reading: An article about the Chicago Fire shows a map with a dark shape stretching from DeKoven Street north across the river. The words say the fire burned more than three square miles. The map shows you what three square miles looks like against the city's grid. That is what a *visual* is for: it says something faster or clearer than the words alone.

Read a graph like a text. Start with the title: what is being measured? Then the labels on the two sides, called axes: what do the numbers stand for, and in what units? Then the scale: does the bottom of the graph start at zero, or is it cut off to make a small change look huge? A bar that looks twice as tall as another may only be a little taller if the scale starts at 90 instead of 0.

Photographs and drawings need the same care. A photo of a burned block after the fire is real evidence, but it shows one block, not the whole city. A caption tells you what the picture maker wants you to see. Ask what is outside the frame. Ask when the picture was taken. A photo of the Water Tower standing alone in the ash tells a story of survival, but the photographer chose that angle.

Finally, connect the visual back to the text. Does the graph support the writer's central idea, or does it quietly show something the writer did not mention? Sometimes the most interesting fact in an article is in a chart the writer barely discussed. A careful reader reads all of it.

words.d: a picture, map, graph or chart that presents information
one of the two labeled lines on a graph that show what is measured
the range of numbers on a graph and the size of the steps between them
the words printed under a picture that explain it

look.title: Two Boxes on the Same Page
look.cite: A one-page article about city budgets, written and counted for this lesson
look.prompt: More than half the numbers on the page are in the chart. What might a reader miss by skipping it?

check.q: What should you check first when reading a graph?
choices: The title and the axis labels, to learn what is measured
Whether it has a photo next to it
check.why: The title and axis labels tell you what the graph measures and in what units. Everything else depends on that.

check.q: A bar graph starts its scale at 90 instead of 0. What can this do?
choices: Make a small difference look huge
check.why: A cut-off scale stretches small differences. Bars can look very different when the real gap is small.

check.q: Why should you ask what is outside the frame of a photograph?
choices: Because the photographer chose what to show, and the rest is missing
Because photos are always older than the text
check.why: A photo shows one angle at one moment. What was left out may change the story.

lessons.title: Fact or Opinion?
lessons.mainIdea: A fact can be checked and shown true or false; an opinion expresses a belief or feeling that cannot be proved, though it can be argued.
reading: "The Chicago Fire started on October 8, 1871." "The Chicago Fire was the worst thing that ever happened to the city." The first sentence is a *fact*. You can check it against records, and it is either true or false. The second is an *opinion*. It states a belief. You could argue for it or against it, but you could never prove it the way you prove a date.

Facts are not always true. "The fire started on October 12" is a fact statement that happens to be false. Fact does not mean true; it means checkable. That matters, because writers sometimes state false things in a confident, factual voice. Your job is not to trust the tone. Your job is to ask: could this be checked, and has it been?

Opinions often come with signal words: I think, I believe, the best, the worst, should, terrible, wonderful. But not always. "Chicago's rebuilding was a triumph" has no I think in it, and it is still an opinion. Look for words that judge, not just words that announce a belief. Words that judge are the fingerprints of opinion.

One more trap. A sentence can mix the two. "The fire, which killed about three hundred people, proved that wooden cities are foolish." The death toll is a fact. Foolish is an opinion. Good readers pull the two apart, accept the fact if it checks out, and weigh the opinion on its own.

words.d: a statement that can be checked and shown to be true or false
a statement of belief or feeling that cannot be proved, though it can be argued

look.title: Sort the Sentences
look.text: 1. Lake Michigan is one of the five Great Lakes. 2. Lake Michigan is the most beautiful of the Great Lakes. 3. Lake Michigan is 307 miles long. 4. Everyone should visit Lake Michigan at least once. 5. Lake Michigan touches four states.
look.prompt: Which sentences are facts and which are opinions? Which fact statements would you want to check, and how?

check.q: What makes a statement a fact?
choices: It can be checked and shown true or false
check.why: A fact is checkable. It may turn out true or false, but it can be tested against evidence.

check.q: "Chicago's rebuilding was a triumph." Why is this an opinion even without the words I think?
choices: Because triumph is a judging word that cannot be proved
Because it uses the past tense
check.why: Words that judge, like triumph, mark an opinion. Signal words like I think are not required.

check.q: A confident writer states something false as a fact. What should a careful reader do?
choices: Assume all of the text is false
Ask whether the statement can be checked and check it
check.why: Tone proves nothing. Fact statements are tested by checking them, not by how sure the writer sounds.

lessons.title: Reasoned Judgment
lessons.mainIdea: A reasoned judgment is a conclusion built from facts and clear reasoning, stronger than a plain opinion but still open to argument.
reading: Between fact and opinion there is a third kind of statement. "Chicago's fire spread so fast mainly because of dry weather, wind and wooden buildings." That is not a checkable fact in the way a date is. But it is not just a feeling either. It is a conclusion drawn from evidence: weather records, wind reports, building materials. Call it a *reasoned judgment*.

A reasoned judgment has two parts you can inspect: the facts it rests on, and the reasoning that connects them to the conclusion. "The teacher blamed the city; therefore the city was at fault" is weak, because one angry witness is thin evidence. "Fire records show most engines were on the east side, and the fire started on the west; therefore the city's placement of engines slowed the response" is stronger. The facts are more solid and the link is clearer.

When you read a judgment, ask three questions. What facts does the writer offer? Are those facts enough to support the conclusion, or is the writer stretching? Is there another conclusion the same facts could support? A judgment that survives all three questions deserves your respect even if you still disagree.

In your own writing, make your judgments reasoned. Do not write "the city was terrible at fighting fires." Write "the city's fire department, with only about seventeen steam engines for a city of some three hundred thousand people, was too small for a wooden city in a dry season." Now a reader can see your facts and follow your reasoning, which is exactly what you want them to do.

words.d: a conclusion supported by facts and clear reasoning, which can still be debated
a decision or belief reached after thinking about evidence
the thinking that connects facts to a conclusion

look.title: One Fact, One Opinion, One Judgment
look.text: The library was open 42 hours a week last year and 30 hours this year. The library is the best place in the neighborhood. Because the library cut twelve hours and the after-school program moved elsewhere, fewer students now have a quiet place to do homework.
look.cite: Three sentences written for this lesson
look.prompt: Label each sentence: fact, opinion or reasoned judgment. For the judgment, name the facts it rests on and the reasoning that links them.

check.q: What makes a reasoned judgment different from a plain opinion?
choices: It is supported by facts and reasoning you can inspect
It uses the words I think
check.why: A reasoned judgment shows its facts and its reasoning. A plain opinion offers only a belief.

check.q: "One witness blamed the city, so the city was at fault." Why is this weak?
choices: Because one witness is thin evidence for a big conclusion
Because the city can never be at fault
check.why: One person's blame is not enough evidence to support a conclusion about the whole city.

check.q: Which question helps you test a writer's judgment?
choices: How many pages is the text?
Could the same facts support a different conclusion?
Does the writer use long words?
check.why: If the facts could point elsewhere, the judgment is weaker. This is one of the three test questions.

review.q: What is the difference between a topic and a central idea?
choices: A topic is a full sentence; a central idea is one word
A topic is what a text is about; a central idea is what the text says about it
A central idea is always a number
review.why: The topic is a word or phrase. The central idea is a full sentence that makes a point about it.

review.q: Which sentence would NOT belong in an objective summary?
choices: The article explains how rip currents form
The writer describes the flags lifeguards use
The article was way too long and boring
The writer gives a drowning statistic
review.why: An objective summary leaves out the reader's opinions and reviews.

review.q: Which pattern uses the signal words both, however and unlike?
review.why: Those signal words show how two things are alike and different.

review.q: "The firefighters crawled toward the blaze." What does the word crawled reveal?
choices: That the firefighters were on their knees
review.why: Crawled suggests slowness and blame. It shows the writer's attitude, which is tone.

review.q: Why did the tailor and the teacher write such different accounts of the same fire?
choices: Their purpose, position and knowledge shaped what each included
review.why: Honest witnesses differ because of where they stood, what they knew and why they wrote.

review.q: A soldier's letter written the night after a battle is
review.why: A letter written at the time by someone who was there is a primary source.

review.q: What can a graph with a scale that starts at 90 instead of 0 do to a reader?
choices: Make the graph easier to read honestly
review.why: A cut-off scale stretches small gaps so bars look far more different than they are.

review.why: The sentence gives facts and connects them to a conclusion, which is a reasoned judgment.
